cards.front: Define osmosis in the specification's words.
cards.back: Water molecules diffuse across a selectively permeable membrane, out of the dilute solution and into the one that is more concentrated.

cards.front: Describe a turgid plant cell.
cards.back: The vacuole is full of water and pushes the cytoplasm and cell membrane hard against the cell wall.

cards.front: Describe a plasmolysed plant cell, in the words the mark scheme wants.
cards.back: The cell membrane has pulled away from the cell wall, because the cell has lost a lot of water.

cards.front: What does the cell wall do when a plant cell is put in pure water?
cards.back: It limits the entry of water: once the cell is turgid the wall will not stretch further, so the cell does not burst.

cards.front: Give the equation for percentage change in mass.
cards.back: Percentage change in mass = change in mass ÷ mass at the start × 100.

cards.front: A chip of potato is left in very salty water. Say what happens to it and why.
cards.back: It loses mass and becomes flaccid: the salty water is more concentrated than the cell sap, so water leaves the cells by osmosis.

cards.front: An animal cell and a plant cell are both put in pure water. How do they end up differently, and why?
cards.back: The animal cell bursts because it has no cell wall; the plant cell becomes turgid because its wall limits the entry of water.

cards.front: In Prescribed Practical B5, why is each cylinder blotted dry before its final weighing?
cards.back: To remove the solution clinging to the surface, which would otherwise be weighed with the cylinder and make the mass too high.

cards.front: Osmosis
cards.back: Diffusion of water molecules from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a selectively permeable membrane.

topics.title: Transpiration, the potometer and uses of water

cards.front: Define transpiration.
cards.back: The evaporation of water from the mesophyll cells, followed by diffusion of the water vapour through the air spaces and out through the stomata.

cards.front: Name the two structures water vapour passes through as it leaves a leaf.
cards.back: The air spaces inside the leaf, and the stomata.

cards.front: List the five factors that affect the rate of transpiration, and say which one lowers it.
cards.back: Surface area, wind, temperature, light intensity and humidity. Humidity is the one that lowers the rate.

cards.front: As light intensity increases, what happens to the rate of transpiration, and why?
cards.back: It increases, because the stomata open for photosynthesis and open stomata let more water vapour out.

cards.front: Why does humidity lower the rate of transpiration?
cards.back: Humid air already holds a lot of water vapour, so the difference in water vapour concentration between the air spaces and the air outside is smaller and the vapour diffuses out more slowly.

cards.front: How is the air bubble in a bubble potometer reset to the start of the scale?
cards.back: Open the tap on the reservoir, or push in the syringe plunger, so water pushes the bubble back.

cards.front: Which way does the potometer bubble move, and why?
cards.back: Towards the shoot: water lost as vapour through the stomata is replaced by water drawn up from the cut end, and the bubble follows the water.

cards.front: How do you turn a bubble's movement into a rate?
cards.back: Subtract the starting reading from the final reading to get the distance moved, then divide by the time taken.

cards.front: Name the four uses a plant makes of water.
cards.back: Support, transport, transpiration and photosynthesis.

cards.front: Why does a cut flower in a vase last longer in a cool, still room than on a sunny windowsill?
cards.back: Cool, still air lowers the rate of transpiration, so the flower loses water more slowly than it can take it up and its cells stay turgid.

cards.front: Describe the washing-line method for investigating water loss from leaves.
cards.back: Weigh cut leaves, hang them up in the conditions being tested, reweigh them after a set time, and work out the mass lost.

cards.front: Why is a layer of oil floated on the water in a weight potometer?
cards.back: To stop water evaporating from the open surface, so the mass lost is only the water the shoot took up.

cards.front: Transpiration
cards.back: Evaporation from mesophyll cells followed by diffusion through air spaces and stomata.

topics.title: Blood components, cell lysis and blood vessels

cards.front: Name the four components of blood and give the function of each.
cards.back: Red cells carry oxygen; white cells defend against disease; platelets convert fibrinogen to fibrin so the blood clots; plasma transports cells, food molecules, carbon dioxide, hormones and urea.

cards.front: Give three adaptations of a red blood cell.
cards.back: Biconcave shape for a large surface area, no nucleus so there is more room inside, and packed with haemoglobin, which contains iron.

cards.front: Name three substances carried in the plasma — and one that is not.
cards.back: Food molecules, carbon dioxide, hormones and urea are carried in the plasma. Oxygen is not: it travels inside the red blood cells.

cards.front: Describe the wall of an artery and say why it is like that.
cards.back: Thick, with muscle and elastic fibres, to withstand the high pressure of blood pumped from the heart and to stretch and recoil with each beat.

cards.front: Describe a vein, and say what its valves do.
cards.back: A thin wall with little muscle and a large lumen; the valves prevent backflow, so blood at low pressure can only travel towards the heart.

cards.front: Give two features of a capillary and say what each allows.
cards.back: Its wall is one cell thick, so substances have a short distance to diffuse, and it is permeable, so materials can be exchanged with the tissues.

cards.front: Higher Tier: what happens to red blood cells put in distilled water, and why?
cards.back: Water enters by osmosis and they burst, because an animal cell has no cell wall to limit the entry of water. This is lysis.

cards.front: How do you calculate a magnification from a drawing?
cards.back: Magnification = drawn size ÷ real size, with both lengths converted to the same unit first. It has no unit.

topics.title: The heart, double circulation and exercise

cards.front: Name the four chambers of the heart and say what each does.
cards.back: The right atrium and left atrium receive blood; the right ventricle pumps it to the lungs and the left ventricle pumps it round the body.

cards.front: Give the route of blood from the body back to the body, in order.
cards.back: vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta.

cards.front: Which artery carries deoxygenated blood, and why is it still an artery?
cards.back: The pulmonary artery. A vessel is an artery because it carries blood away from the heart, not because of the blood inside it.

cards.front: Why is the left ventricle wall thicker than the right?
cards.back: It pumps blood all the way round the body, which needs a higher pressure; the right ventricle only pumps as far as the lungs.

cards.front: What do the valves in the heart do?
cards.back: They prevent backflow, so blood can only flow in one direction through the heart.

cards.front: Name the vessels of the liver and the kidney.
cards.back: Hepatic artery in and hepatic vein out for the liver, plus the hepatic portal vein from the intestine; renal artery in and renal vein out for the kidney.

cards.front: Give the equation for cardiac output.
cards.back: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate.

cards.front: State the two ways the circulatory system benefits from regular exercise.
cards.back: The heart muscle is strengthened, and the cardiac output when at rest increases.

cards.front: Why does the blood pass through the heart twice on every circuit?
cards.back: Blood leaving the lungs is at low pressure after the capillaries there, so it returns to the heart to be pumped again and reach the whole body quickly.

cards.front: Which blood vessels supply the heart muscle itself?
cards.back: The coronary arteries, which branch off the aorta and run over the surface of the heart.

cards.front: Name the six parts of the male reproductive system the specification lists.
cards.back: Testis, scrotum, sperm tube, prostate gland, urethra and penis.

cards.front: What does the prostate gland do?
cards.back: It adds fluid to the sperm. Sperm and that fluid together are called semen.

cards.front: The urethra and the ureter are two different tubes. What does each one carry, and where does it run?
cards.back: The urethra carries semen and, at other times, urine, and runs from the bladder out through the penis. The ureter carries urine only, from the kidney down to the bladder.

cards.front: Name the five parts of the female reproductive system the specification lists.
cards.back: Ovary, oviduct, uterus, cervix and vagina.

cards.front: Where does fertilisation happen, and where does the ball of cells settle afterwards?
cards.back: Fertilisation happens in the oviduct. The ball of cells settles into the lining of the uterus.

cards.front: Why are the testes held in the scrotum, outside the body?
cards.back: Because it is cooler outside the body, and sperm are made best at a temperature a little below body temperature.

topics.title: Sex hormones and the menstrual cycle

cards.front: Name the two sex hormones the specification lists, and the organ that makes each one.
cards.back: Testosterone, made in the testes, and oestrogen, made in the ovaries.

cards.front: What does oestrogen do in the menstrual cycle, and what does progesterone do?
cards.back: Oestrogen repairs and thickens the lining of the uterus. Progesterone maintains that lining through the second half of the cycle.

cards.front: Menstruation happens on days ___ to ___ of a 28-day cycle, and ovulation happens at about day ___.
cards.back: Menstruation happens on days 1 to 5, and ovulation happens at about day 14.

cards.front: Day 1 of the menstrual cycle is which day exactly?
cards.back: Day 1 is the first day of bleeding, not the day the bleeding ends.

cards.front: A cycle lasts 32 days. Ovulation is about 14 days before the end of a cycle. On about which day does ovulation happen?
cards.back: About day 18, because 32 − 14 = 18. The fourteen days are counted back from the end of the cycle, so a longer cycle ovulates later.

cards.front: Give two secondary sexual characteristics caused by testosterone and two caused by oestrogen.
cards.back: Testosterone: a deeper voice and the growth of facial hair. Oestrogen: the breasts develop and the hips widen.

cards.front: What happens to the lining of the uterus if the ovum is not fertilised?
cards.back: The level of progesterone falls, so the lining is no longer maintained. It breaks down and is lost, which is menstruation, and day 1 of the next cycle begins.

cards.front: On a hormone graph with no numbers on the vertical axis, what can you read and what can you not?
cards.back: You can read the timing: when each curve rises, peaks and falls. You cannot compare the heights of two different hormones, because the axis has no scale.

cards.front: How does the contraceptive pill prevent pregnancy?
cards.back: It changes hormone levels, and that stops an ovum developing so none is released.

cards.front: Name CCEA's three groups of contraception and give one method in each.
cards.back: Mechanical: the condom. Chemical: the contraceptive pill, or an implant. Surgical: sterilisation.

cards.front: What can a condom do that the contraceptive pill cannot?
cards.back: A condom also prevents the spread of sexually transmitted infections, such as HIV and chlamydia, because only a barrier stops something passing between two people.

cards.front: Which tube is cut in male sterilisation, and which in female sterilisation?
cards.back: The sperm tubes are cut in male sterilisation, so sperm cannot leave. The oviducts are cut in female sterilisation, so the ovum and the sperm cannot meet.

cards.front: Describe in vitro fertilisation in three steps, as the specification states it. (Higher Tier)
cards.back: Hormones are used to produce multiple ova; the ova are fertilised in a dish in the laboratory; and several embryos are transferred into the uterus.

cards.front: A question asks for an ethical reason why someone might not use contraception. What kind of answer earns the mark?
cards.back: A religious or moral reason: something the person believes to be right or wrong. Cost, side effects and reliability are practical reasons, not ethical ones.

topics.title: Sperm, fertilisation, implantation and the placenta

cards.front: What is a zygote, and how is it different from an embryo?
cards.back: A zygote is the single diploid cell formed when the haploid sperm and egg nuclei fuse. An embryo is the many cells that form once that zygote has divided by mitosis.

cards.front: What is the difference between implantation and differentiation?
cards.back: Implantation is a change of place: the ball of cells settles into the lining of the uterus. Differentiation is a change of job: the cells become different from one another to form tissues and organs.

cards.front: Give three adaptations of a sperm cell, and the reason for each one.
cards.back: A haploid nucleus, so that fertilisation restores the diploid number; mitochondria, which release the energy for swimming; and a flagellum, which makes the sperm swim to the ovum.

cards.front: Where does fertilisation take place, and what exactly happens there?
cards.back: In the oviduct. The haploid nucleus of the sperm and the haploid nucleus of the ovum fuse to give a diploid zygote.

cards.front: How is the placenta adapted for diffusion? Give three points, each with its reason.
cards.back: The villi give a large surface area, so more diffusion happens at once; the barrier between the two blood supplies is thin, so the diffusion distance is short; and the good blood supply on both sides keeps the difference in concentration up.

cards.front: Name the four substances the specification says cross the placenta, and say which way each one goes.
cards.back: Dissolved nutrients and oxygen cross to the foetus; carbon dioxide and urea cross from the foetus to the mother.

cards.front: What do the umbilical cord, the amnion and the amniotic fluid each do?
cards.back: The umbilical cord carries blood, and so the substances in it, to and from the foetus. The amnion is the membrane around the foetus, and the amniotic fluid inside it cushions the foetus.

cards.front: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. How many are in a sperm cell, and how many in the zygote it helps to form?
cards.back: 23 in the sperm, because a gamete is haploid, and 46 in the zygote, because the two haploid nuclei fuse and the zygote is diploid.

sections.title: 2.4 Genome, Chromosomes, Genes, DNA and Genetics

topics.title: Genome, chromosomes, genes, alleles and DNA structure

cards.front: What is the genome of an organism?
cards.back: The genome is all of the genetic material of an organism.

cards.front: Define a gene, and then define an allele.
cards.back: A gene is a short length of DNA on a chromosome that controls a characteristic. An allele is a different form of the same gene.
keyWords: different form of the same gene

cards.front: A human body cell holds ___ chromosomes, in ___ functional pairs. A gamete holds ___.
cards.back: A human body cell holds 46 chromosomes, in 23 functional pairs. A gamete holds 23.

cards.front: Which two kinds of cell do NOT hold their chromosomes in functional pairs?
cards.back: Gametes, which carry one of each pair, and bacteria, which have no nucleus.

cards.front: Describe the structure of DNA in one sentence.
cards.back: A phosphate and sugar (deoxyribose) backbone with interlinking bases, twisted into a double helix.

cards.front: State the base-pairing rules.
cards.back: A pairs with T, and C pairs with G.

cards.front: In a length of DNA, 20% of the bases are A. What percentage are G?
cards.back: 30%. A pairs with T, so T is 20% as well, which is 40% used. That leaves 60% for C and G together, and they are equal, so G is 30%.

cards.front: Higher tier: how do you turn a number of bases into a number of amino acids?
cards.back: Divide by three, because a base triplet of three bases codes for one amino acid.

cards.front: Genome
cards.back: The entire genetic material of an organism.

cards.front: Allele
cards.back: A different form of the same gene.

cards.front: Give the four numbers for mitosis: divisions, cells, chromosome number, and how alike the cells are.
cards.back: One division, two cells, the same chromosome number as the parent, and the cells are genetically identical clones.

cards.front: Give the four numbers for meiosis: divisions, cells, chromosome number, and how alike the cells are.
cards.back: Two divisions, four cells, half the chromosome number, and all four are genetically different.

cards.front: Give the three uses of mitosis that the specification lists.
cards.back: Growth, replacing worn-out cells and repairing damaged tissue.

cards.front: Name the process in meiosis that reassorts the chromosomes, and say what it produces.
cards.back: Independent assortment, and it produces variation.

cards.front: A human body cell holds ___ chromosomes; a gamete holds ___; a zygote holds ___.
cards.back: A human body cell holds 46 chromosomes; a gamete holds 23; a zygote holds 46.

cards.front: Where in the human body does meiosis take place, and what does it make there?
cards.back: Only in the ovaries and the testes, where it makes the gametes.

cards.front: Why is meiosis called a reduction division, and what does haploid mean?
cards.back: Because it halves the chromosome number. A haploid cell holds one chromosome from each pair.

cards.front: A body cell of a cat holds 38 chromosomes. How many are in one of its ova, and how many in a cell of its skin?
cards.back: 19 in an ovum, because meiosis halves the number, and 38 in a skin cell, because mitosis keeps it.

cards.front: How do you test whether a drawn nucleus could have been produced by meiosis?
cards.back: Check that it holds exactly one chromosome from each pair: one of the long pair and one of the short pair, in any combination.

cards.front: What is a clone, and which kind of cell division makes one?
cards.back: A cell genetically identical to the cell it came from, made by mitosis.

cards.front: Meiosis
cards.back: Reduction division: one cell producing four genetically different haploid daughter cells.

cards.front: Mitosis
cards.back: Exact duplication of chromosomes producing daughter cells genetically identical to the parent cell.

topics.title: Monohybrid crosses, Punnett squares, test crosses and pedigrees

cards.front: Define genotype and phenotype.
cards.back: The genotype is the alleles an organism carries for a characteristic. The phenotype is the characteristic you can see.

cards.front: Give the three terms for the genotypes BB, bb and Bb, where B is dominant.
cards.back: BB is homozygous dominant, bb is homozygous recessive and Bb is heterozygous.

cards.front: Give the four steps of working out a cross, in order.
cards.back: Parents' genotypes, then gametes, then the offspring in the square, then count what the question asks for.

cards.front: How many alleles does a gamete carry for one characteristic, and why?
cards.back: One, because meiosis puts one chromosome of each pair into each gamete.

cards.front: What phenotype ratio does a cross between two heterozygous parents give, and what percentage shows the recessive phenotype?
cards.back: 3 : 1, and 25% show the recessive phenotype.

cards.front: What is the difference between a phenotype ratio and a genotype ratio for one gene with two alleles?
cards.back: The phenotype ratio has two numbers, 3 : 1, because the two dominant genotypes look alike. The genotype ratio has three, 1 : 2 : 1, because it counts them apart.

cards.front: Describe a test cross in one sentence, and say what each result proves.
cards.back: Cross the unknown with a homozygous recessive animal: any recessive offspring proves it is heterozygous, and all-dominant offspring point to homozygous dominant.

cards.front: On a pedigree diagram, which individuals give you a certain genotype straight away?
cards.back: The ones showing the recessive phenotype: they must be homozygous recessive.

cards.front: In tomato plants, tall (T) is dominant to short (t). Two Tt plants are crossed. What fraction of the offspring is expected to be short?
cards.back: One quarter, because only tt gives a short plant and one box in four is tt.

cards.front: A question's part (b) names its own two parents. What must you do with the genotypes from part (a)?
cards.back: Leave them behind. Each part names the animals it is about, and carrying the earlier pair over loses the mark.

topics.title: Sex determination, inherited conditions and genetic screening

cards.front: A human female has the sex chromosomes ___ and a human male has ___.
cards.back: A human female has the sex chromosomes XX and a human male has XY.

cards.front: Which sex chromosomes are in a germ cell in a man's testis, and which in one sperm cell?
cards.back: An X and a Y in a germ cell; an X or a Y in each sperm cell, because meiosis gives each sperm one of the pair.

cards.front: What ratio of boys to girls does the sex-determination square give, and why is it the same for every pregnancy?
cards.back: 1 : 1, a 50% chance either way, because half the father's sperm carry a Y every time.

cards.front: Give the cause of each of the four conditions CCEA names.
cards.back: Cystic fibrosis: a recessive allele. Huntington's disease: a dominant allele. Down's syndrome: an extra copy of chromosome 21. Haemophilia (Higher): a recessive allele carried on the X chromosome.

cards.front: A person with Down's syndrome has ___ chromosomes in each body cell, because there are ___ copies of chromosome 21.
cards.back: A person with Down's syndrome has 47 chromosomes in each body cell, because there are 3 copies of chromosome 21.

cards.front: Which genotypes can a person with Huntington's disease have?
cards.back: Homozygous dominant or heterozygous: one copy of the dominant allele is enough.

cards.front: What is a carrier of cystic fibrosis, and what is the chance that two carriers have a child with it?
cards.back: Someone with one copy of the recessive allele who does not have the condition. Two carriers have a 25% chance of an affected child.
keyWords: one copy of the recessive allele

cards.front: Higher tier. Why does haemophilia affect far more males than females?
cards.back: A male has one X chromosome, so one haemophilia allele is enough; a female with one has a normal allele on her other X and is only a carrier.

cards.front: Describe how amniocentesis is carried out, in three steps.
cards.back: A needle is pushed into the uterus; a sample of amniotic fluid is taken; the foetal cells in it are tested.

cards.front: Name the four ethical issues of genetic screening that the specification lists.
cards.back: Who decides who is tested; the risks of amniocentesis against the benefits of a blood test; the dilemma for a carrier after a diagnosis; and making genetic information available to wider society, such as insurance companies.

cards.front: What is genetic engineering?
cards.back: Changing the genome of an organism to give it a desirable characteristic.

cards.front: Name the type of enzyme that cuts the insulin gene out of human DNA, and name the ends it leaves.
cards.back: A restriction enzyme, and it leaves sticky ends.

cards.front: Why is the same restriction enzyme used on the human DNA and on the plasmid?
cards.back: It cuts at the same base sequence both times, so the sticky ends are complementary and the gene can join the plasmid.

cards.front: A restriction enzyme finds its site n times along a straight length of DNA. How many sections are made? And on a ring?
cards.back: A straight length gives n + 1 sections, because it already has two ends. A ring gives n pieces, because the first cut only opens it.

cards.front: What makes a restriction enzyme's cut staggered?
cards.back: It cuts the two strands at different points, a few bases apart, which leaves single-stranded sticky ends.

cards.front: What is a recombinant plasmid?
cards.back: A plasmid that has had a gene from another organism joined into it: here, the human insulin gene.

cards.front: Does the plasmid carry insulin or the insulin gene into the bacterium?
cards.back: The insulin gene. The bacterium makes the insulin from it afterwards.

cards.front: What happens to the modified bacteria and their plasmids in the fermenter?
cards.back: They multiply: the bacteria reproduce, the plasmids are copied, and each bacterium makes human insulin.

cards.front: What are the three stages of downstreaming, and why is it needed?
cards.back: Extraction, purification and packaging. It is needed so that a pure form of insulin reaches the patient.

cards.front: Give three advantages of making human insulin with genetically modified bacteria.
cards.back: It is identical to human insulin, it can be made in large quantities and cheaply, and no animal is used.

topics.title: Continuous and discontinuous variation; genetic and environmental causes

cards.front: What is continuous variation, and which graph displays it?
cards.back: A characteristic that can take any value in a range, such as height. It is displayed on a histogram, with the bars touching.

cards.front: What is discontinuous variation, and which graph displays it?
cards.back: A characteristic that falls into a few separate groups, such as tongue rolling. It is displayed on a bar chart, with gaps between the bars.

cards.front: Why do the bars of a histogram touch but the bars of a bar chart do not?
cards.back: A histogram shows measured data: every value in between is possible, so one class runs into the next. A bar chart shows separate groups with nothing in between.

cards.front: Name the two causes of variation that have a genetic basis.
cards.back: Mutation and sexual reproduction.

cards.front: What is a mutation?
cards.back: A random change in the number of chromosomes or in the structure of a gene.

cards.front: Two cuttings from one plant grow to different heights. Why must the cause be environmental?
cards.back: Cuttings from one plant have the same genes, so any difference between them comes from the environment, such as water or light.

sections.title: 2.6 Health, Disease, Defence Mechanisms and Treatments

topics.title: Health, communicable diseases and aseptic technique

cards.front: Define health, in the words of the CCEA specification.
cards.back: Health is being free from communicable and non-communicable disease.

cards.front: Name the three diseases on the specification that are caused by bacteria.
cards.back: Chlamydia, salmonella and tuberculosis.

cards.front: Name the diseases on the specification that are caused by viruses.
cards.back: HIV, which leads to AIDS; cold and flu; and HPV.

cards.front: Name the two diseases on the specification that are caused by fungi, and say how each spreads.
cards.back: Athlete's foot, picked up from damp floors and shared towels, and potato blight, whose spores travel on wind and rain.

cards.front: Why can antibiotics not treat flu?
cards.back: Flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics only kill bacteria.

cards.front: Give two costs of disease to society.
cards.back: The NHS pays for treatment (GP visits, medicines, hospital beds and staff), and working days are lost.

cards.front: What is sterilised in an autoclave, and how is the inoculating loop sterilised?
cards.back: Petri dishes, culture media and culture bottles go in the autoclave; the loop is heated in a Bunsen flame until it glows red hot.

cards.front: During inoculation, why is a Petri dish opened only a crack, and beside a Bunsen burner?
cards.back: To stop microorganisms from the air landing on the agar and contaminating it; the rising hot air above the flame carries them away.

cards.front: What is the maximum temperature for incubating cultures in school, and why?
cards.back: 25 °C, to avoid growing pathogens, which grow best near body temperature.

cards.front: Health
cards.back: Being free from communicable and non-communicable disease.
